sources.title: Knowledge Tracing: Modeling the Acquisition of Procedural Knowledge
Original diagnostic scenarios and distractor analysis for the AI foundations seed corpus
sources.notes: All stems, options, rationales, and misconception formulations are original synthesis. Canonical references support concepts rather than verbatim wording.

questions.stem: A hospital trains a model to predict 30-day readmission at the moment a patient is admitted. Its table has one row per admission and includes length_of_stay, which is known only at discharge. Some patients have multiple admissions. Which evaluation redesign most directly makes the reported performance credible for future patients?

options.text: Remove post-admission features, split by patient and chronology, and fit preprocessing within each training partition.
options.rationale: This aligns feature availability, independence units, time direction, and learned preprocessing with the intended admission-time deployment.

options.text: Keep length_of_stay because it is not the target, but stratify a random row split by the readmission label.
options.rationale: A non-target feature still leaks if it is unavailable when the prediction must be made; stratification does not repair that.

options.text: Keep the feature set and use leave-one-admission-out cross-validation so that each row is tested exactly once.
options.rationale: More folds do not prevent the same patient or later-time information from crossing boundaries, and the post-admission feature remains invalid.

options.text: Remove the explicit readmission column, standardize all remaining rows together, and then create the train-test split.
options.rationale: Fitting scaling before the split leaks held-out distribution information and still fails to audit prediction-time availability.

questions.stem: A team tries 40 hyperparameter configurations. After each run it inspects performance on the same nominal test set and chooses the configuration with the highest test accuracy. What is the strongest correction if the goal is an honest final performance estimate?

options.text: Report the best test accuracy because searching more configurations makes the maximum estimate conservative.
options.rationale: Choosing the maximum of many noisy test estimates creates optimism; a larger search usually worsens the winner's curse.

options.text: Select configurations on validation data, lock the workflow, then evaluate once on an untouched test set; use nested cross-validation when data are scarce.
options.rationale: Model-selection feedback is separated from the final estimate; nested cross-validation reproduces that separation across outer folds.

options.text: Average the 40 test accuracies so that positive and negative selection errors cancel before reporting the chosen model, despite choosing it from those same repeated measurements.
options.rationale: Averaging candidate scores does not undo that test feedback determined which model and workflow were selected.

options.text: Continue using the test set for selection, but rename it validation after the final configuration has been chosen.
options.rationale: Renaming correctly acknowledges its role but does not create a new untouched set for final evaluation.

questions.stem: An L2-regularized logistic regression is refit with the same numerical penalty strength after one feature is converted from meters to millimeters. The physical information is unchanged. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Predictions should be identical because an invertible rescaling can be absorbed into the corresponding coefficient.
options.rationale: The score can be reparameterized, but the L2 norm of that reparameterized coefficient is different, so the penalized optimum need not match.

options.text: The effect is limited to convergence speed; feature units do not change the optimum of a convex logistic-regression objective under penalization.
options.rationale: Convexity guarantees the nature of the optimum, not invariance of an objective whose penalty changes under coordinate rescaling.

options.text: Predictions can change because the rescaling changes the penalty geometry; standardize within training data or transform the penalty and retune it.
options.rationale: L2 applies to coordinate values, so changing units changes relative shrinkage unless scaling or per-coordinate penalties compensate.

options.text: Multiplying the one global penalty strength by 1000 exactly restores the original solution for all coefficients.
options.rationale: A global change also alters shrinkage on untouched features and cannot exactly undo a change isolated to one coordinate.

questions.stem: A deep decision tree has almost zero training error. Across repeated, deployment-aligned cross-validation splits, its validation error ranges from 12% to 31%, and the selected root features change substantially. What is the best diagnosis and response?

options.text: The model has high bias; increasing tree depth should reduce both the split variability and validation error across future samples as well.
options.rationale: Near-zero training error argues against an underfitting diagnosis, while greater depth usually increases sensitivity to sample details.

options.text: The model has low variance because its training error is stable; merely the average validation error matters.
options.rationale: Variance concerns changes in the fitted function across samples, which the unstable validation results and roots directly reveal.

options.text: Choose the split with 12% error as representative and discard the other splits as unlucky partition noise.
options.rationale: Selecting the most favorable split produces another selection bias and hides the uncertainty the repeats were intended to expose.

options.text: The pattern indicates high variance; constrain or prune the tree, or use variance-reducing aggregation, and retain uncertainty across valid resamples.
options.rationale: Unstable fitted structure plus a wide validation range is characteristic of estimation variance; regularization or bagging targets that sensitivity.

questions.stem: A calibrated model outputs p = P(disease | x). A false negative costs 20 units, a false positive costs 1 unit, and correct decisions have zero cost. Ignoring capacity constraints, when should the system predict disease?

options.text: Predict disease when p > 1/21, because the expected false-positive cost then falls below the expected false-negative cost.
options.rationale: Positive costs 1(1-p), negative costs 20p, and 1-p < 20p exactly when p > 1/21.

options.text: Predict disease when p > 1/2, because calibrated probabilities should use the class with greater posterior probability.
options.rationale: The maximum-posterior rule is optimal only under a matching symmetric-cost setup, which is explicitly absent here.

options.text: Predict disease when p exceeds disease prevalence, because prevalence is the correct cutoff for an imbalanced outcome.
options.rationale: Prevalence affects the posterior distribution but the action indifference point here is determined by the stated cost ratio.

options.text: Choose the threshold that maximizes F1, because F1 by itself weights a false negative twenty times more heavily in this setting.
options.rationale: F1 does not contain the stated 20-to-1 cost ratio and need not maximize expected utility.

questions.stem: On a deployment-matched validation set, model A has ROC AUC 0.92 and expected calibration error 0.14; model B has ROC AUC 0.84 and expected calibration error 0.02. The system must rank patients and also trigger an intervention when stated risk exceeds 30%. Which conclusion is sound?

options.text: Model A dominates for both uses because an AUC above 0.9 establishes trustworthy probability values at deployment.
options.rationale: AUC measures ordering, not whether a displayed 0.30 risk corresponds to an event frequency near 30%.

options.text: A ranks better, but its 30% cutoff needs calibration validation; monotone recalibration can preserve its ranking.
options.rationale: The two uses demand different properties, and a monotone recalibration can improve probability semantics while preserving order.

options.text: Model B has higher precision throughout the threshold range because better calibration entails better discrimination.
options.rationale: Calibration quality does not impose threshold-by-threshold ranking dominance; the lower AUC is evidence against that claim.

options.text: Recalibrating model A necessarily changes its ROC AUC substantially, so ranking and probability repair do not separate.
options.rationale: Strictly monotone recalibration preserves pairwise ordering and therefore ordinarily preserves ROC AUC.

questions.stem: A diagnostic classifier moves from a specialty clinic to population screening. Careful audits indicate that p(x | y) is stable for both disease states, but disease prevalence p(y) changes substantially. Which shift is described?

options.text: No shift, because stable class-conditional feature distributions imply the complete joint distribution is unchanged.
options.rationale: The joint p(x,y)=p(x|y)p(y) changes when p(y) changes even if p(x|y) remains fixed.

options.text: Covariate shift, because any resulting change in the marginal distribution p(x) receives that name.
options.rationale: Although p(x) may consequently change, the stated invariant factorization is the defining label-shift setup.

options.text: Label shift, because p(y) changes while the class-conditional feature mechanism p(x | y) remains stable.
options.rationale: This is precisely the prior-probability or label-shift assumption.

options.text: Concept shift, because a prevalence change means the predictive relationship p(y | x) changed for structural reasons.
options.rationale: The posterior may numerically change through Bayes' rule, but the stipulated change is in priors, not a changed class-conditional mechanism.

questions.stem: In observational school data, students assigned tutoring improve less on average than students without tutoring. Assignment is targeted toward students whom teachers expect to struggle. A flexible predictor reproduces the negative association after controlling for many recorded variables. What can be concluded about the effect of offering tutoring?

options.text: Tutoring is harmful because accurate prediction of the observed association estimates the intervention effect.
options.rationale: The model estimates an observational conditional association, while targeted assignment can confound the treatment comparison.

options.text: Tutoring is beneficial because controlling for many variables by itself removes all sources of confounding.
options.rationale: Adjustment works only for a justified set under assumptions; variable count alone neither establishes direction nor identification.

options.text: Collecting enough additional records will reveal the causal effect even if assignment remains governed by the same unmeasured judgments.
options.rationale: More samples can tighten an association estimate but do not resolve unmeasured confounding or non-identifiability.

options.text: The causal effect is not identified here; estimating it requires a credible design or explicit assumptions about assignment.
options.rationale: Targeted treatment creates confounding by indication, so predictive fit does not answer the interventional question without identification.

questions.stem: Gradient descent on a convex quadratic loss zigzags along a steep direction but advances very slowly along a shallow direction. The Hessian has a large ratio between its largest and smallest eigenvalues. Which intervention most directly addresses the cause?

options.text: Rescale, whiten, or precondition the coordinates to improve the condition number, then retune the step size.
options.rationale: The pathology is anisotropic curvature; a coordinate transformation or preconditioner directly makes progress more even across directions.

options.text: Use an extremely small learning rate; once oscillation stops, convergence is equally fast in all eigendirections.
options.rationale: A smaller step can stabilize the steep direction but makes progress along the shallow direction even slower.

options.text: Run the same update longer, because repeated gradients gradually reduce the Hessian's condition number.
options.rationale: For a fixed quadratic, the Hessian and its condition number do not improve merely because more iterations are executed.

options.text: Add momentum with any coefficient; momentum algebraically changes the quadratic to condition number one.
options.rationale: Momentum may accelerate a tuned optimization but neither guarantees perfect conditioning nor removes the need to respect curvature.

questions.stem: A computation is h = f_theta(x), z = stop_gradient(h), prediction = g_phi(z), followed by a scalar loss. Neither parameter set is used elsewhere. What happens during backpropagation?

options.text: Neither theta nor phi receives a gradient, because detaching z disconnects everything after h from the loss.
options.rationale: The loss remains differentiably connected to phi through g; only the backward edge from z to h is blocked.

options.text: Phi receives its ordinary gradient, while theta receives zero through this path; the forward value of z still equals h.
options.rationale: Stop-gradient is identity in the forward pass and has zero derivative at the detached edge in the backward pass.

options.text: Theta receives a gradient because h influenced the prediction value, while phi receives none because z is treated as constant.
options.rationale: Forward influence does not cross a detached backward edge, whereas treating z as constant still permits differentiation with respect to phi.

options.text: Both parameter sets update normally because stop_gradient modifies the forward tensor value but leaves its derivative unchanged.
options.rationale: This reverses the operator's definition: its value is unchanged, but its derivative toward h is set to zero.

questions.stem: A self-attention layer uses shared query, key, and value projections but no positional encodings or position-dependent mask. If the input token rows are permuted, what happens to the token outputs and to a classifier that mean-pools those outputs?

options.text: Token outputs remain in their original order because global attention reconstructs absolute positions from pairwise scores.
options.rationale: Pairwise content scores contain no absolute index signal; global access alone does not break permutation symmetry.

options.text: Token outputs change arbitrarily because the learned projection matrices are tied to fixed row indices.
options.rationale: The projections are shared across rows, so permuting input rows simply permutes Q, K, V, and the corresponding outputs.

options.text: Token outputs are permuted in the same way, and mean pooling produces the same classifier input as before.
options.rationale: Unpositioned self-attention is permutation equivariant, and mean pooling converts that equivariance into permutation invariance.

options.text: Token outputs are equivariant, but mean pooling recovers the original sequence order and therefore changes the classifier input.
options.rationale: Mean pooling is symmetric and cannot recover or react to row order.

questions.stem: A standard full self-attention block keeps hidden width, head count, batch size, and weights fixed while sequence length increases from L to 2L. Ignoring implementation-specific kernels, which scaling statement is most accurate?

options.text: Parameters and attention work both roughly double, because each additional token is processed once.
options.rationale: Token projections are linear in L, but the full query-key and attention-value interactions involve L squared pairs.

options.text: Parameters and attention work both roughly quadruple, because the model learns one weight set per token pair.
options.rationale: Pairwise activations grow quadratically, but projection and feed-forward weights are shared across positions and do not grow with input length.

options.text: Training attention roughly quadruples, but inference attention merely doubles because no gradient tensors are stored.
options.rationale: Backward storage affects constants and memory, not the L squared pairwise computation required by the full forward pass.

options.text: Parameters stay fixed; pairwise attention terms grow about fourfold, while token-wise projection work grows about twofold.
options.rationale: Weights are length independent, L-by-L terms scale quadratically, and per-token operations scale linearly.

questions.stem: Naive Bayes can outperform logistic regression with little data when its assumptions are useful, while logistic regression may win with more data when those assumptions are violated. Which explanation uses the generative-discriminative distinction correctly?

options.text: Naive Bayes models p(x | y)p(y), while logistic regression models p(y | x) directly; their different assumptions create different sample-efficiency tradeoffs.
options.rationale: Generative assumptions can reduce estimation burden when useful but introduce misspecification costs; discriminative fitting focuses directly on the conditional task.

options.text: A model is generative when a neural decoder can synthesize realistic raw examples, so Naive Bayes is not generative under the standard probabilistic definition of generation.
options.rationale: Generative refers to modeling a joint or data distribution; it does not require a neural architecture or photorealistic sampling.

options.text: A discriminative classifier does not output probabilities because it models a boundary rather than p(y | x).
options.rationale: Logistic regression is a discriminative model precisely because it directly parameterizes a conditional probability.

options.text: Estimating p(x, y) requires fewer assumptions than estimating p(y | x), so the generative model eventually dominates.
options.rationale: A joint model estimates more structure and generally makes additional commitments that may be useful or misspecified.

questions.stem: A dataset contains a dollar-valued feature with enormous variance and several standardized biomarker features with smaller variance. The label is mainly separated along a low-variance biomarker direction. A team applies PCA before classification. Which practice is best justified?

options.text: Retain the highest-variance components because PCA orders directions by their ability to separate any downstream label in later prediction tasks.
options.rationale: PCA does not inspect labels, so a low-variance direction can carry most of the predictive signal.

options.text: Scale by domain meaning, fit PCA within training folds, and choose dimension by held-out prediction rather than variance.
options.rationale: Scaling defines the variance geometry, fold-local fitting avoids leakage, and the supervised objective determines whether compression helps.

options.text: Skip scaling because PCA eigenvectors are invariant to changing a feature from dollars to cents.
options.rationale: Changing units rescales covariance contributions and can rotate principal directions toward the rescaled feature.

options.text: Retain all principal components because adding components does not worsen a downstream model's expected generalization.
options.rationale: More components can restore noise and estimation variance; finite-data generalization must be validated.

questions.stem: Customer observations form two curved, interleaving regions with unequal density. Features mix dollar amounts and unitless ratios. K-means produces unstable segments. Which response best matches the evidence?

options.text: Increase k until the curved regions emerge, because k-means is a density method for arbitrary cluster shapes.
options.rationale: K-means partitions space by centroid proximity and does not directly model curved, variable-density regions.

options.text: Choose the k with maximum silhouette score and treat those groups as the uniquely true customer segments.
options.rationale: Silhouette evaluates one distance-based partition criterion; it does not establish unique semantic reality.

options.text: Define meaningful scaling, try a graph- or density-based method, and test stability and business usefulness under those explicit assumptions.
options.rationale: The geometry violates k-means assumptions, units distort distance, and unsupervised groups require stability plus external interpretation.

options.text: Replicate the ratio columns until they match the dollar range; k-means distances are otherwise invariant to feature scale or units.
options.rationale: Replication and rescaling both reweight distance contributions; neither is an invariant or automatically meaningful correction.

questions.stem: Logged clinical decisions came from a behavior policy that never selected treatment A for a particular region of patient states. A target policy selects A there with positive probability. With no additional data, what is the central obstacle to unbiased off-policy evaluation?

options.text: There is no obstacle: assign zero importance weight to the unsupported target decisions and the estimate remains unbiased.
options.rationale: The required target-to-behavior ratio has a positive numerator and zero denominator; dropping those decisions removes target-policy mass.

options.text: Fit any dynamics model and evaluate A in simulation; model-based estimation removes the need for behavioral coverage.
options.rationale: A model can extrapolate, but unsupported action effects then depend on untestable modeling assumptions rather than nonparametric identification.

options.text: Average the observed behavior-policy returns because both policies operate in the same environment and therefore have the same value.
options.rationale: Different actions change state visitation and rewards, so behavior-policy returns do not directly estimate the target policy.

options.text: The positivity or support condition fails; the target value is not identified there without new coverage or defensible extrapolation assumptions.
options.rationale: Off-policy estimators need behavior support wherever the target assigns probability; otherwise the missing counterfactual outcomes are not observed.

questions.stem: A discounted MDP has discount gamma and a sparse goal reward. Which dense reward transformation has the standard policy-invariance guarantee, assuming bounded state potential Phi and otherwise unchanged dynamics?

options.text: Use r'(s,a,s') = r(s,a,s') + gamma Phi(s') - Phi(s), with terminal handling consistent with the potential definition.
options.rationale: The discounted potential differences telescope in returns, shifting state values without changing the ordering of action values within a state.

options.text: Add a positive bonus whenever distance to the goal decreases, because a locally progressive reward preserves optimality.
options.rationale: An arbitrary progress bonus can change path preferences or create exploitable cycles unless it has the required potential form.

options.text: Use r'(s,a,s') = r(s,a,s') + Phi(s') - Phi(s); the discount factor is irrelevant to telescoping in discounted trajectory returns.
options.rationale: In a discounted return, cancellation requires gamma Phi(s') for the next-state term.

options.text: Use any bounded dense reward that preserves the ranking of terminal states, despite intermediate paths and cycles.
options.rationale: Optimal policies depend on full discounted trajectory returns, not only the ordering of terminal rewards.

questions.stem: Let H1 be contained in a richer hypothesis class H2. Both models are fit by exact empirical risk minimization on the same finite training sample. Which statement follows without assuming the sample equals the deployment distribution perfectly?

options.text: The H2 solution has no greater training risk and therefore has no greater population risk.
options.rationale: The first clause follows from nesting; the population-risk conclusion does not because the selected richer model can have a larger estimation gap.

options.text: H2 has no higher minimum training risk, but either class may generalize better because estimation error can offset approximation gains.
options.rationale: Class inclusion guarantees only empirical monotonicity; finite-sample generalization depends on how selection interacts with complexity and noise.

options.text: Exact ERM directly minimizes population risk, so H2 is guaranteed to match or outperform H1 in deployment.
options.rationale: ERM minimizes a sample average; the inaccessible population expectation is a different quantity.

options.text: Once a validation set exists, H2 may be searched without limit because validation removes complexity and selection effects under repeated reuse.
options.rationale: A finite validation set can itself be overfit through sufficiently adaptive search and does not erase estimation uncertainty.

questions.stem: An MCQ requires both conditional-probability reasoning and calibration knowledge. A learner answers incorrectly. The item model includes nonzero slip and guess probabilities, and neither skill is known with certainty. Which learner-state update is most defensible?

options.text: Set mastery of both skills to zero, because an incorrect response proves all required components were absent.
options.rationale: The response could arise from one missing skill, both, or a slip; hard-zeroing both overstates the evidence.

options.text: Mark the highest-weight skill alone as unmastered, because a content weight identifies the unique cause of failure.
options.rationale: Concept weights describe item relevance, not observed causal attribution for this individual response.

options.text: Use Bayes' rule with the multi-skill response likelihood, retaining uncertainty over mastery, slips, guesses, and failure attribution.
options.rationale: A probabilistic observation model uses the response as noisy evidence and avoids pretending that a multi-skill item isolates one latent cause.

options.text: Leave both skill posteriors unchanged, because evidence involving more than one concept does not update either concept validly.
options.rationale: Ambiguity weakens attribution but does not make the response uninformative under a specified multi-skill likelihood.

questions.stem: An adaptive tutor has a posterior over a learner's concepts and a bank with calibrated item-response models. It must choose the next MCQ for both diagnosis and learning while avoiding repetition. Which policy is the strongest default?

options.text: Choose the bank's hardest item each time, because maximum difficulty produces maximum information for any learner.
options.rationale: An item far above the learner can yield an almost certain incorrect response and little discrimination among plausible learner states.

options.text: Choose any item whose concept mastery is closest to 0.5, without considering its response model, prerequisites, or instructional value during selection.
options.rationale: Posterior uncertainty matters, but an item can be weakly discriminating, premature, or pedagogically unhelpful.

options.text: Repeatedly choose the single item with greatest immediate information gain, with no content balancing or exposure limits.
options.rationale: Unconstrained greedy selection can overexpose an item family, neglect coverage, and harm engagement or learning.

options.text: Optimize expected information gain or learning value under prerequisite, coverage, exposure, diversity, and fatigue constraints, then update from the observed response.
options.rationale: This uses the learner posterior and item model while recognizing that a useful tutor has pedagogical and operational constraints beyond pure uncertainty reduction.

questions.stem: A standardized two-dimensional dataset has two compact groups and one extremely distant observation. Repeated k-means fits pull one centroid toward that observation and split a compact group inconsistently. Which diagnosis and response best match the objective being optimized?

options.text: Squared distances give the extreme point high leverage; inspect it and compare a robust transform, trimmed objective, or medoid-based method.
options.rationale: K-means minimizes within-cluster squared distance, so a remote point can dominate the objective; the proposed checks directly address that sensitivity.

options.text: The behavior shows k-means has become density-based; use k-means++ initialization to remove the distant point's influence on fitted centroids.
options.rationale: Initialization can improve a local solution but does not turn the centroid objective into a density method or remove squared-distance leverage.

options.text: Because inputs were standardized once, returning one coordinate to its original units would leave the fitted centroids and partition unchanged.
options.rationale: Changing a coordinate's scale changes its squared-distance contribution and can alter centroid locations, assignments, and the apparent outlier influence.

options.text: A high silhouette score would establish the recovered groups as real; retain whichever value of k maximizes that score on this sample.
options.rationale: An internal score describes geometry under a chosen metric; it does not establish external reality or robustness to the influential point.

questions.stem: A team proposes customer segments from one k-means fit. You need to determine whether the segmentation is a reproducible structure rather than an artifact of initialization or sampling. Which evaluation is most informative?

options.text: Express high-variance features in several measurement units and expect identical memberships, because coordinate scaling leaves k-means geometry unchanged.
options.rationale: K-means uses Euclidean squared distance, so rescaling coordinates can change the partition rather than provide a neutral stability check.

options.text: Refit across resamples and initializations, align memberships with a permutation-invariant agreement measure, and check whether stable groups support the intended use.
options.rationale: This tests reproducibility while handling arbitrary labels and supplements geometric stability with the segmentation's external purpose.

options.text: Choose the fit with the largest silhouette score on the original data and treat that internal optimum as evidence of reproducible segments.
options.rationale: A single-sample internal optimum does not test sensitivity to resampling or initialization and does not validate the intended interpretation.

options.text: Replace resampling with density-contour inspection, because k-means estimates density modes whose identities persist across samples and initializations.
options.rationale: K-means minimizes a centroid distortion objective rather than estimating density modes, and visual contours do not quantify resampling stability.

questions.stem: Centered observations have covariance eigenvalues 9, 4, and 1. PCA retains the first two principal components. What fraction of total sample variance is represented by the retained two-dimensional projection?

options.text: The fraction is 5/6, about 83.3%, because explained variation is obtained by summing the principal-direction standard deviations.
options.rationale: The square roots 3, 2, and 1 are standard deviations, whereas explained variance ratios use the covariance eigenvalues.

options.text: The fraction is 9/10, or 90%, because PCA normalizes coordinate scale before calculating variance and removes the smallest feature's units.
options.rationale: Ordinary covariance PCA does not silently standardize coordinates; explained variance is the sum of retained eigenvalues divided by their total.

options.text: The fraction is 13/14, about 92.9%, because the retained covariance eigenvalues sum to 13 while total variance is 14.
options.rationale: The trace of the covariance matrix is total variance, and each retained eigenvalue is variance along its principal direction.

options.text: The fraction is undetermined until labels are supplied, because PCA measures how much class separation the first two directions preserve.
options.rationale: PCA is unsupervised and its explained-variance calculation depends on the feature covariance, not class labels.

questions.stem: A PCA report says the first score is 0.70 times centered height plus 0.70 times centered weight, while software on another run prints both loadings as negative. Which interpretation is statistically defensible?

options.text: The second run found the opposite substantive relationship, because the global sign of each principal-component loading has an identified interpretation across software implementations.
options.rationale: An eigenvector and its negation describe the same axis, so global sign flips do not change the projected geometry.

options.text: Converting weight from kilograms to grams leaves both 0.70 loadings unchanged, because PCA geometry is invariant to feature measurement units.
options.rationale: Covariance PCA is scale-sensitive, so a large unit conversion can rotate the principal directions unless standardization is applied deliberately.

options.text: The displayed component should be supplemented by the remaining components in prediction, because retaining more principal components improves expected generalization.
options.rationale: Extra components preserve more sample variance but may add noise and estimation variance for a particular supervised task.

options.text: The score is a rotated linear combination; relative loading patterns can aid interpretation, while a simultaneous sign flip leaves the component axis unchanged.
options.rationale: This distinguishes the meaningful relative composition of a component from its arbitrary global orientation.

questions.stem: A logistic classifier uses log odds z = -2 + x1 + x2 and predicts class 1 when its estimated probability is at least 0.5. Which statement correctly describes its probability surface and decision boundary?

options.text: Probability is the sigmoid of z, so it varies nonlinearly; the 0.5 boundary is the affine line x1 + x2 = 2.
options.rationale: The sigmoid maps zero log odds to probability 0.5, and setting the affine score to zero yields the stated line.

options.text: Probability equals z directly, so the classifier has a linear probability surface and the boundary is x1 + x2 = 0 throughout feature space.
options.rationale: The affine expression is a log-odds score, not a probability; the intercept also shifts its zero level.

options.text: Probability is the sigmoid of z, but changing the classification threshold leaves the same line x1 + x2 = 2.
options.rationale: A different probability threshold corresponds to a different log-odds level and therefore shifts the parallel decision line.

options.text: No probability boundary is defined, because a discriminative classifier produces class scores without a valid conditional probability interpretation.
options.rationale: Logistic regression directly parameterizes a conditional class probability even though it does not model the feature distribution.

questions.stem: A neural classifier estimates p(y given x) accurately on its deployment population, but its designers never specified a model for p(x). What can and cannot be inferred from this discriminative model alone?

options.text: Its conditional probabilities determine p(x) through normalization, so samples of realistic features can be generated directly from the classifier.
options.rationale: Normalizing across labels at a fixed x supplies no probability mass across different feature values.

options.text: It can support label decisions for observed x under a stated loss, but p(x) and the full joint distribution remain unspecified.
options.rationale: A conditional classifier is sufficient for many prediction decisions, while a joint model would additionally require a feature marginal.

options.text: It does not classify an observed x coherently for prediction until a separate feature generator supplies p(x) and completes the joint distribution.
options.rationale: Conditional probabilities can be used directly for Bayes decisions once x is observed and the decision loss is specified.

options.text: Its outputs are nonprobabilistic scores, because probabilistic predictions arise from generative models that specify both labels and features.
options.rationale: Discriminative models can produce valid conditional probabilities without supplying a generative feature model.

questions.stem: A rare-event logistic model is trained with positive examples weighted twenty times more than negative examples. Its ranking is useful, but predicted values greatly exceed observed event frequencies on representative validation data. What is the strongest explanation and remedy?

options.text: Class weights affect optimizer speed rather than the population target; continue training until the raw values match validation frequencies on representative data.
options.rationale: Class-dependent weights change the pointwise loss optimum, so convergence does not restore the unweighted posterior.

options.text: Weighted log loss still estimates unshifted population probabilities; the frequency mismatch therefore proves the validation labels are unreliable.
options.rationale: The weighting changes the odds represented by the optimal score, so systematic overprediction is compatible with reliable validation labels.

options.text: Class weighting shifts the effective posterior odds; undo the known shift or recalibrate on representative held-out data before reporting probabilities.
options.rationale: This preserves possible ranking benefits while restoring probability semantics using the weighting relation or unbiased calibration evidence.

options.text: Choose a larger classification threshold and report the unchanged raw values, because threshold selection also calibrates the numeric probabilities.
options.rationale: A decision threshold changes class assignments but does not alter or calibrate the probability values shown to users.

questions.stem: A model class contains constant predictions only, and the observed targets are 1, 2, and 100. How does changing the empirical loss from squared error to absolute error change the fitted constant?

options.text: Both losses fit 34 and one third, because empirical risk minimization selects the sample mean independently of the chosen loss.
options.rationale: The empirical objective includes the loss definition, so changing that definition can change its minimizer.

options.text: Squared error fits 2, while absolute error fits 34 and one third, because squared residuals target the sample median.
options.rationale: Squared loss is minimized at the arithmetic mean; the median is the constant solution for absolute loss.

options.text: Squared error fits 34 and one third, while absolute error also fits that value because absolute residuals target the sample mean.
options.rationale: Absolute-error slopes balance at a median, which is 2 for this ordered three-point sample.

options.text: Squared error fits 34 and one third, while absolute error fits 2; the loss determines which empirical summary is optimal.
options.rationale: The sample mean minimizes summed squared deviations, whereas any sample median minimizes summed absolute deviations.

questions.stem: A team minimizes average training loss plus lambda times the squared coefficient norm, choosing lambda on a finite validation set. Which statement most accurately describes what this procedure optimizes and what remains uncertain?

options.text: For fixed lambda it minimizes a penalized sample objective; validation selects among such fits, while deployment risk still has estimation uncertainty.
options.rationale: The statement distinguishes data fit, an explicit parameter preference, validation-based selection, and the unknown population expectation.

options.text: Among candidate lambdas, the fit with lower training loss also has lower deployment risk, so validation evidence is unnecessary for selection.
options.rationale: Training loss omits the estimation gap, so a less constrained fit can improve sample fit while worsening population performance.

options.text: After lambda is chosen on validation, further complexity control and selection accounting are unnecessary because validation prevents adaptive overfitting.
options.rationale: A finite validation set can itself be overfit through broad adaptive search, and its selection uncertainty remains relevant.

options.text: Choosing lambda on validation turns the selected sample objective into population risk, eliminating the estimation gap for the final hypothesis.
options.rationale: Validation provides finite evidence for selection but does not make an unknown deployment expectation identical to a sample quantity.

questions.stem: A nearest-neighbor model uses age measured in years and annual income measured in dollars. Without scaling, income differences dominate Euclidean distance. What does standardizing these coordinates actually do?

options.text: It leaves the distance geometry unchanged and improves floating-point precision, because standardization is a numerical implementation detail.
options.rationale: Coordinate scaling changes relative distance contributions and can therefore change neighbor identities, not merely arithmetic conditioning.

options.text: It defines a different metric in which one standard-deviation change in each feature has comparable coordinate weight before model fitting.
options.rationale: Standardization rescales axes and thereby encodes a substantive notion of proximity for a Euclidean algorithm.

options.text: It adds predictive information by converting dollars into standardized units, creating distinctions that were absent in the original observations for downstream learning.
options.rationale: An invertible rescaling preserves information in the data even though a scale-sensitive algorithm may use that information differently.

options.text: It changes convergence speed while preserving the selected neighbors, because scaling affects optimization but not distance-based model geometry.
options.rationale: Nearest-neighbor selection is itself defined by distances, so rescaling can directly change predictions without an iterative optimizer.

questions.stem: A linear predictor contains beta times x. The feature is replaced by x-prime = 100x, and the coefficient is adjusted to preserve fitted values. Under an unchanged L2 penalty lambda times beta squared, what follows?

options.text: The adjusted coefficient remains beta, because changing feature units leaves the numerical coefficient invariant when predictions are preserved.
options.rationale: To preserve beta times x after multiplying x by 100, its coefficient must be divided by 100.

options.text: The adjusted coefficient is beta over 100, and its L2 contribution stays equal because equivalent predictions imply equivalent penalties.
options.rationale: The prediction is preserved, but squaring the rescaled coefficient makes this term ten thousand times smaller.

options.text: The adjusted coefficient is beta over 100, preserving predictions, while its unchanged-form L2 penalty becomes ten thousand times smaller.
options.rationale: Substitution gives beta-prime x-prime = beta x with beta-prime = beta/100, but coefficient norms are not invariant to that reparameterization.

options.text: The adjusted coefficient is 100 beta, and the larger penalty is a numerical side effect that leaves the regularized solution unchanged.
options.rationale: Multiplying both feature and coefficient changes predictions by a factor of ten thousand, and penalty geometry can change the fitted solution.

questions.stem: A positive affine unit conversion is applied to one continuous feature before fitting several model families. Which comparison best captures why the consequence of scaling depends on the learning algorithm?

options.text: Each model family needs standardized inputs for statistical validity, so the same conversion has essentially the same effect across algorithms.
options.rationale: Scale sensitivity follows from the model and fitting procedure; it is not a shared validity requirement across model families.

options.text: A standard decision tree changes its attainable partitions because the conversion changes feature ordering, while Euclidean methods preserve their distances.
options.rationale: A positive affine conversion preserves order and translates tree thresholds, whereas it changes relative Euclidean coordinate contributions.

options.text: The conversion alters the information carried by that feature, so any performance difference reflects information gained or lost during rescaling.
options.rationale: An invertible unit conversion preserves information; algorithmic geometry and parameter priors explain different fitted behavior.

options.text: Tree split membership can remain equivalent because order is preserved, while distances, coefficient penalties, and gradient conditioning can change materially.
options.rationale: This traces invariance or sensitivity to the actual operations used by each algorithm instead of applying a universal scaling rule.

questions.stem: A regression model predicts y-hat = beta-zero + beta-one x + beta-two x-squared. The fitted curve can bend as x changes. In what precise sense is this still a linear model?

options.text: It is linear in the unknown coefficients applied to the fixed basis features 1, x, and x-squared, despite curvature in raw x.
options.rationale: Linear-model terminology concerns the coefficients' entry into the predictor; transformed inputs can represent nonlinear raw-input shapes.

options.text: It stops being linear when x-squared is included, because a linear model permits untransformed first-power input columns in the design matrix.
options.rationale: A fixed nonlinear feature map does not prevent the predictor from remaining linear in its fitted coefficients.

options.text: It is linear because beta-two becomes a nonlinear parameter whose value changes with x to trace the quadratic response curve.
options.rationale: The fitted coefficient beta-two is a fixed parameter; the basis value x-squared changes with the observation.

options.text: It is linear on the response scale because equal steps in x produce equal changes in y-hat after adding the quadratic basis term.
options.rationale: With a nonzero quadratic coefficient, equal raw-input steps generally produce different response changes.

questions.stem: Two predictors in a linear regression are nearly duplicates. Repeated samples produce very different individual coefficients, yet fitted values for observations in the same predictor region change little. Which interpretation is best?

options.text: Near collinearity makes the fitted values unusable, because unstable individual coefficients invalidate predictions throughout the observed predictor region.
options.rationale: Some linear combinations can be estimated stably for in-support prediction even when attribution to individual columns is unstable.

options.text: The data identify their combined predictive direction better than their separate effects; coefficient attribution is unstable even when in-support predictions are stable.
options.rationale: Nearly redundant columns create a weakly identified coefficient direction while preserving fitted values along directions supported by the data.

options.text: Stable fitted values establish that each coefficient is well identified, and the across-sample variation is evidence of harmless optimizer randomness in repeated samples.
options.rationale: Strong aggregate prediction does not identify how association should be divided between nearly duplicate predictors.

options.text: Dropping either predictor preserves the remaining coefficient's substantive meaning, because correlated variables carry interchangeable interpretations as well as information.
options.rationale: Removing a correlated variable changes the conditioning set and can reallocate shared association to the retained coefficient.

questions.stem: A linear model fits plant growth well for temperatures from 15 to 30 degrees Celsius. A user requests a prediction at 80 degrees, far beyond observed support. Which response correctly separates computation from evidence?

options.text: The linear form validates the 80-degree prediction under deployment, because a straight relationship has the same slope beyond the observed temperature range.
options.rationale: The assumed equation extends algebraically, but the observed data do not establish that its slope persists under extreme conditions.

options.text: The model returns the response observed near 30 degrees, because linear predictions are clipped at the largest training feature value.
options.rationale: An ordinary affine predictor continues its equation outside the feature range unless clipping is added explicitly.

options.text: The equation produces a number at 80 degrees, but its reliability depends on unsupported structural assumptions and domain behavior beyond the sample.
options.rationale: This distinguishes the ability to evaluate a formula from empirical or scientific support for extrapolating that formula.

options.text: Low training error validates the extrapolation, because accurate interpolation demonstrates that the same mechanism governs unobserved extreme temperatures.
options.rationale: In-range residuals provide no direct observations of the relationship at 80 degrees and cannot rule out regime changes.

questions.stem: In a screened population, disease prevalence is 1%, sensitivity is 90%, and the false-positive rate is 9%. For a randomly selected person who tests positive, what is the approximate probability of disease?

options.text: About 90%, because sensitivity is the probability that a person has disease after receiving a positive result.
options.rationale: Sensitivity conditions on disease, whereas the requested posterior conditions on the observed positive test.

options.text: About 50%, because a positive result overrides the initial rarity and places disease and nondisease on equal footing.
options.rationale: The low prevalence produces many more nondiseased people who can contribute false positives.

options.text: About 91%, because one minus the false-positive rate is the fraction of positive results that are true positives.
options.rationale: One minus the false-positive rate is specificity, whose denominator is nondiseased people rather than positive tests.

options.text: About 9.2%, because among 10,000 people there are about 90 true positives and 891 false positives, giving 90 divided by 981.
options.rationale: Expected-count Bayes reasoning makes the denominator explicit and yields a posterior near 0.0917.

questions.stem: Two laboratory tests are independent conditional on a patient's disease status. Each test is more likely positive when disease is present. Before disease status is observed, how are the two test results generally related?

options.text: They are generally positively associated: one positive raises belief in disease, which raises the predictive probability that the other test is positive.
options.rationale: Mixing conditionally independent tests over a common latent cause can induce marginal dependence through posterior updating.

options.text: They remain marginally independent, because conditional independence continues after the disease variable is averaged out of the joint distribution.
options.rationale: Averaging over disease mixes groups with different positive rates and generally creates dependence between the test results.

options.text: They are unrelated through disease, because a shared latent cause changes individual test rates without inducing association between observed outcomes.
options.rationale: Variation in the shared disease state moves both positive probabilities together and therefore induces marginal association.

options.text: They have identical sensitivities and false-positive rates, because conditional independence requires both tests to use the same conditional distribution.
options.rationale: Conditional independence factorizes the joint distribution but permits the two tests to have different conditional parameters.

questions.stem: A random variable X equals negative one or positive one with equal probability, and g(x) = x-squared. Which comparison between E[g(X)] and g(E[X]) is correct, and what principle does it illustrate?

options.text: Both equal zero, because expectation can be moved through the square before evaluating the two possible outcomes.
options.rationale: Linearity of expectation does not permit replacing the expectation of a square by the square of the expectation.

options.text: E[g(X)] equals one while g(E[X]) equals zero; expectation generally does not commute with a nonlinear transformation.
options.rationale: Each realized square is one, but the symmetric random variable has mean zero, whose square is zero.

options.text: Both equal zero because zero is the expected and therefore most likely value of X before the square is applied.
options.rationale: Zero is the mean but is not in the support of this random variable, and each realized square equals one.

options.text: The values here are one and zero, and matching mean and variance would determine E[g(X)] for any nonlinear g in other distributions.
options.rationale: The numerical pair is right here, but arbitrary nonlinear expectations can depend on higher moments and distributional shape.

questions.stem: A learner summarizes three probability lessons involving diagnostic tests, shared latent causes, and nonlinear transformations. Which combined summary is valid across all three settings?

options.text: Sensitivity gives disease probability after a positive test, while shared causes and nonlinear transformations require separate distributional calculations.
options.rationale: The first clause reverses conditioning; posterior disease probability also depends on prevalence and the false-positive process.

options.text: Conditional independence persists marginally after a shared cause is hidden, while Bayes calculations and nonlinear expectations use their stated distributions.
options.rationale: Marginalizing a common cause can associate variables that factorize after conditioning on that cause.

options.text: Bayes denominators use base rates, shared latent causes can induce marginal dependence, and nonlinear expectations require averaging transformed outcomes.
options.rationale: Each clause preserves the relevant conditioning direction or distributional operation without collapsing distinct probability concepts.

options.text: Expectation can pass through nonlinear transformations, while base rates and shared causes affect diagnostic-test calculations in their usual way.
options.rationale: The expectation identity holds for affine transformations but not for a general nonlinear function.

questions.stem: A recommender chooses daily lessons. Today's choice affects what the learner understands tomorrow, which lessons become useful, and the later rewards observed by the system. Why is this not adequately framed as ordinary supervised prediction of today's reward?

options.text: Each observed reward is a fixed label for the chosen lesson, so minimizing one-step prediction error solves the learning problem.
options.rationale: A reward is policy-dependent feedback within a trajectory, not a fixed counterfactual label for all available actions.

options.text: Future lesson data follow an external sampling process, so today's action changes immediate reward without changing later states or observations.
options.rationale: The scenario explicitly makes future understanding, useful choices, and collected data depend on the current action.

options.text: A later reward should be assigned to the most recent lesson, so earlier choices can be removed from the credit calculation.
options.rationale: Earlier actions can alter the state path that produces delayed outcomes, so temporal credit cannot be assigned by recency alone.

options.text: Actions influence future states and the data distribution, while delayed returns couple a current choice to later consequences under the continuing policy.
options.rationale: These are the sequential intervention and delayed-return features that distinguish reinforcement learning from passive labeled prediction.

questions.stem: In a two-action bandit, action A has one unlucky initial reward and then a greedy policy repeatedly chooses action B because its current estimate is higher. What is the core failure, and what kind of response addresses it?

options.text: The policy receives no new evidence about A after abandoning it; deliberate exploration or uncertainty-aware selection can trade short-term reward for information.
options.rationale: Greedy lock-in is caused by endogenous missing information, and exploration gives uncertain actions a route to be reevaluated.

options.text: The policy will sample A as time passes, because a greedy rule accumulates exploration evidence even for actions it does not choose.
options.rationale: Elapsed time provides no reward observations for an action whose selection count remains fixed.

options.text: Uniform random action choice is the optimal remedy, because directed exploration does not improve the information-regret tradeoff over equal sampling.
options.rationale: Random exploration is a baseline, while uncertainty-aware methods can direct samples toward actions where information has greater value.

options.text: Accurate reward prediction on logged B actions establishes A's value, so additional action support is unnecessary before changing the policy.
options.rationale: Predictions on observed B outcomes do not identify counterfactual rewards for an action with inadequate support.

questions.stem: An agent receives reward 2 immediately after its current action and reward 4 one step later, with no further rewards and discount factor gamma = 0.5. What is the return from the current time?

options.text: The return is 3, computed as 0.5 times 2 plus 0.5 times 4, because discounting starts on the immediate reward.
options.rationale: The immediate reward has temporal offset zero and therefore coefficient gamma to the zero power, which is one.

options.text: The return is 4, computed as 2 plus 0.5 times 4, because the next-step reward receives one factor of gamma.
options.rationale: Discounted return begins with the immediate reward and applies gamma once to a reward one step later.

options.text: The return is 6, computed as 2 plus 4, because gamma represents random termination rather than weighting delayed rewards in this trajectory.
options.rationale: Whatever probabilistic interpretation gamma may have, the return definition directly weights the delayed reward by gamma.

options.text: The current return stays the same after swapping rewards 2 and 4, because discounted value depends on reward amounts rather than temporal order.
options.rationale: Swapping the rewards gives 4 plus 0.5 times 2, which is 5 rather than the original return of 4.

questions.stem: A learner summarizes sequential decision making, exploration, and discounting. Which combined statement preserves the essential distinction in all three parts?

options.text: Actions change immediate reward but leave future data fixed; exploration and discounting then operate on an externally supplied trajectory distribution.
options.rationale: In sequential control, actions can change state transitions and therefore the future observations available to the learner.

options.text: A greedy policy gathers evidence about abandoned actions as time passes, while discounting handles delayed outcomes after that passive exploration.
options.rationale: An unchosen action supplies no new reward evidence, so a strictly greedy policy can remain locked into an early error.

options.text: Actions shape future experience, exploration buys information about uncertain choices, and discounting weights rewards according to their delay from the current decision.
options.rationale: The statement correctly connects policy-dependent data, the value of information, and the temporal indexing of return.

options.text: Actions shape future experience and exploration buys information, but gamma first discounts the reward received immediately after the current action.
options.rationale: The immediate reward has exponent zero in the standard return; gamma first appears on the next delayed reward.

questions.stem: A deployed nearest-neighbor pipeline standardizes each feature. During evaluation, which procedure preserves the meaning of a held-out prediction without letting that observation influence the fitted geometry?

options.text: Estimate each center and scale from the training fold, then apply those fixed values to its validation fold and later deployment observations.
options.rationale: The fitted transform is part of the learned pipeline, so validation and deployment observations must be mapped with training-derived parameters.

options.text: Estimate centers and scales from the complete dataset, since standardization changes numerical representation without changing the model's effective geometry.
options.rationale: Standardization defines coordinate weights for a distance model, and using held-out values to fit those weights contaminates evaluation.

options.text: Re-estimate the transform separately for each new observation, since expressing a value in fresh standardized units adds information about its deployment context.
options.rationale: An observation-specific transform changes comparability to the reference data; invertible rescaling does not create new predictive information.

options.text: Standardize each pipeline by convention, since all model families require zero-centered unit-variance features for statistically valid predictions.
options.rationale: The need for a fitted transform depends on the model geometry; it is not a universal condition for statistical validity.

questions.stem: A ridge model uses two features, and one feature is converted from meters to millimeters. The team wants the same set of fitted prediction functions to receive the same objective values. What must it do?

options.text: Keep both coefficients and penalty weights fixed, because converting a measurement unit leaves the numerical coefficients and objective terms unchanged.
options.rationale: The converted feature needs an inversely rescaled coefficient even before accounting for the coefficient penalty.

options.text: Rescale the affected coefficient inversely and transform its penalty weight accordingly; preserving predictions alone does not preserve an isotropic coefficient norm.
options.rationale: A unit conversion is a parameter reexpression, and the regularizer must be transformed with it to preserve objective equivalence.

options.text: Rescale the affected coefficient inversely but retain one common penalty weight, because prediction-equivalent parameterizations necessarily incur equal regularization costs.
options.rationale: An ordinary coefficient norm depends on parameter units, so equal fitted values can carry unequal penalty values.

options.text: Keep the original objective and lower the optimizer step size, because scaling can alter convergence speed but not the regularized solution being selected.
options.rationale: A smaller step size can stabilize optimization but cannot restore an objective whose penalty geometry changed under reparameterization.

questions.stem: Two predictors encode equally useful signals, but one is measured on a scale one hundred times larger. A lasso fit uses one common penalty coefficient without standardization. Which consequence is most plausible?

options.text: Selection is unaffected because coefficients attached to useful signals retain the same numerical values after any invertible feature rescaling.
options.rationale: Preserving a feature's contribution requires its coefficient to change inversely with the feature's numerical scale.

options.text: Selection is unaffected because prediction-equivalent coefficients receive equal absolute-value penalties even when their feature units differ by a factor of one hundred.
options.rationale: The lasso penalty acts on numerical coefficients, so two equivalent predictive contributions can have different penalty costs.

options.text: The larger-scale predictor can represent the same contribution with a smaller coefficient and may therefore be favored by the unadjusted lasso penalty.
options.rationale: With a shared coefficient penalty, raw feature scale can alter which predictive directions are cheaper and therefore which variables survive.

options.text: The fitted sparse model is unchanged and merely converges at a different rate, since scaling influences optimization without influencing feature selection.
options.rationale: The penalty is part of the objective, so scale-dependent coefficient costs can change the selected solution itself.

questions.stem: One k-means cluster contains one-dimensional observations at 0, 0, 0, and 20. With assignments held fixed for the update step, where is the squared-distance minimizing centroid, and what does it reveal?

options.text: It is 0, because a k-means centroid is a robust center that stays at the majority location despite one extreme observation.
options.rationale: The arithmetic mean, not the median or mode, minimizes the within-cluster sum of squared distances.

options.text: It is near 20, because k-means follows the highest-density location and the isolated point forms the sharpest local density peak.
options.rationale: The centroid update averages assigned coordinates; it does not seek a mode of an estimated density.

options.text: Its location is chosen by whichever candidate gives the largest silhouette value, which identifies the true center for this observed cluster.
options.rationale: Silhouette is an evaluation summary, whereas the fixed-assignment k-means update has a direct least-squares minimizer.

options.text: It is 5, the arithmetic mean; the movement away from the three zeros shows the leverage that squared distance gives the outlier.
options.rationale: Differentiating the sum of squared deviations gives the sample mean, and the value 20 moves that mean from zero to five.

questions.stem: Two clustering runs assign every observation to exactly the same companions, but one run names the groups 1 and 2 while the other swaps those names. How should their agreement be evaluated?

options.text: Treat the partitions as equivalent by aligning labels or using a permutation-invariant agreement measure, since the numeric names carry no cluster identity.
options.rationale: A clustering is a partition, and relabeling its blocks does not change which observations are grouped together.

options.text: Treat the runs as disagreements because label 1 denotes a fixed population group whose identity persists across initializations and samples.
options.rationale: Ordinary clustering labels are arbitrary identifiers; direct numeric comparison confuses a renaming with a membership change.

options.text: Increase the requested cluster count until both runs retain matching numeric names, because additional groups resolve instability caused by label switching.
options.rationale: Changing the number of blocks does not give arbitrary numeric labels semantic identity and can introduce new instability.

options.text: Choose the run with the larger internal score and call its numeric labels correct, because an internal optimum establishes the canonical partition naming.
options.rationale: An internal score does not make label names canonical or establish that one observed partition is uniquely true.

questions.stem: Noise-free points lie on two concentric circular rings in two equally scaled coordinates. The desired groups are the inner and outer rings. Which modeling decision best matches that structure?

options.text: Use ordinary k-means because its centroid objective is density-based and therefore separates any two disconnected high-density curves into their natural rings.
options.rationale: K-means creates Voronoi regions around centroids and can cut each ring into angular pieces rather than recover nested curves.

options.text: Use a graph, spectral, or suitable density method whose neighborhood assumptions can represent nested groups, then test sensitivity to its scale choices.
options.rationale: The desired membership follows connectivity along curved manifolds, which can be encoded by neighborhood-based methods rather than centroid Voronoi cells.

options.text: Multiply one coordinate by a large constant, because feature scaling leaves k-means memberships invariant while forcing its centroids to follow circular boundaries.
options.rationale: Anisotropic rescaling changes Euclidean geometry but does not convert centroid Voronoi regions into concentric ring boundaries.

options.text: Increase k until each ring receives a stable numeric label, because additional centroids necessarily resolve mismatches between cluster shape and objective.
options.rationale: More centroids can approximate ring fragments while still failing to produce the requested two connected ring memberships.

questions.stem: On four binary training examples, two classifiers make the same four hard class predictions, but one assigns much higher probability to each observed label. How can their empirical zero-one and log losses compare?

options.text: Both empirical losses tie because zero-one loss and log loss share an optimizer whenever the classifiers produce the same hard labels.
options.rationale: Zero-one loss discards probability confidence, while log loss distinguishes the probability assigned to the observed label.

options.text: Their log losses tie because empirical risk minimization ignores the selected loss once the model class and training observations are fixed.
options.rationale: Empirical risk is defined by the chosen loss, so identical hard predictions need not imply identical probabilistic loss.

options.text: Their zero-one losses tie, while the more confident correct classifier has lower log loss because log loss retains probability information beyond the decision.
options.rationale: The two losses summarize different aspects of the same fitted outputs and can therefore rank the classifiers differently.

options.text: The lower training log loss proves lower deployment loss, because improving a finer empirical score eliminates uncertainty about future examples from the target process.
options.rationale: A lower sample objective is not a guarantee about an unknown population expectation, even when the loss is strictly proper.

questions.stem: For a fixed training sample, increasing the coefficient on a norm penalty changes the fitted parameter and raises the unpenalized training loss. Which interpretation of this regularized empirical fit is sound?

options.text: The penalty contributes synthetic labeled observations, so its coefficient literally increases the empirical sample size used by the risk calculation.
options.rationale: A penalty adds a parameter preference to the objective; it does not add observed feature-label pairs to the sample.

options.text: The penalty leaves the empirical minimizer unchanged and merely records a complexity score after the unpenalized training solution has been selected.
options.rationale: When included during optimization, the penalty trades data fit against parameter size and can move the minimizing parameter.

options.text: The new fit directly minimizes deployment risk, because adding a norm converts the finite-sample objective into the unknown population expectation.
options.rationale: Regularization can improve expected generalization but does not make a sample objective identical to population risk.

options.text: It minimizes a different empirical objective that trades sample fit for norm size; an equivalent constrained form can bound the allowed parameter norm.
options.rationale: Penalized and suitably constrained formulations express the same fit-versus-complexity tradeoff under standard convex conditions.

questions.stem: A linear regression represents a three-level category with an intercept and two indicator columns. The analyst changes which category is the reference level and refits the same model space. What should happen?

options.text: The coefficient meanings and values change with the reference, while fitted group means can remain identical because the represented prediction space is unchanged.
options.rationale: Reference coding reparameterizes the same group-mean model; coefficients become different contrasts without changing attainable fitted values.

options.text: The model ceases to be linear because indicator features are nonlinear transformations that a linear design matrix does not legitimately contain.
options.rationale: Linearity concerns how fixed design columns combine with coefficients, and indicator columns are valid basis features.

options.text: The original coefficient values persist because an equally good fit uniquely identifies each individual coefficient under any parameter coding.
options.rationale: A fit can be represented with different intercepts and contrasts when the reference basis changes.

options.text: The coefficients become observation-dependent nonlinear parameters, and that parameter nonlinearity is what preserves the same fitted means after recoding.
options.rationale: The coefficients remain fixed numbers; preservation comes from changing the basis and its coefficient representation together.

questions.stem: A regression design includes an intercept plus all three indicators for a three-level category, making one column an exact linear combination of the others. What is the precise consequence?

options.text: The fitted group predictions are invalid, because any exact collinearity destroys the model's ability to represent stable in-sample fitted values.
options.rationale: Rank deficiency prevents unique coefficient attribution but can still permit uniquely determined fitted values in the column space.

options.text: Multiple coefficient vectors produce the same fitted values; removing a redundant column or imposing a constraint selects an identifiable parameterization.
options.rationale: The null direction changes coefficients without changing the linear predictor, so an additional coding convention is needed for uniqueness.

options.text: A high training fit chooses one substantively identified coefficient vector, because predictive accuracy resolves the exact dependency among design columns.
options.rationale: All vectors differing along the null direction have the same fitted values and therefore the same training fit.

options.text: Dropping any indicator preserves the remaining coefficients' original interpretations, because redundant columns are interchangeable in both information and meaning.
options.rationale: Choosing a reference changes coefficient contrasts even though it can preserve the represented group predictions.

options.text: It is x = 0.8, because the model probability is the same linear quantity as its log-odds score throughout the feature space.

options.text: It remains x = 0, because changing a classification threshold changes labels without moving the decision boundary of a logistic model.
options.rationale: The 0.5 boundary occurs at log odds zero, while a threshold of 0.8 requires positive log odds.

options.text: Continue optimization longer, because altered class proportions influence convergence speed but leave the fitted population probability target unchanged.

options.text: The coordinates are independent, because orthogonal principal axes remove linear and nonlinear forms of statistical dependence between their scores.

options.text: A and B remain tied under both values, because the order of a fixed pair of reward amounts does not affect discounted return.

options.text: A changes from return 1 to return 0.5 while B changes from return 1 to return 0.5, because gamma discounts immediate rewards first.

options.rationale: Return from the current decision weights later rewards by their temporal distance rather than assigning them solely by recency.

options.text: It is 80%, because sensitivity is the probability of disease after positive evidence and a second positive leaves that interpretation unchanged.
options.rationale: Sensitivity conditions on disease, while the requested posterior also depends on prevalence and false positives among nondiseased people.

options.text: It is 50%, because two positive results balance disease and nondisease evidence once the original base rate is removed from the calculation.
options.rationale: The prior odds remain a factor in the posterior even after multiple likelihood contributions are observed.

options.text: It is 96%, because one minus the joint false-positive probability of 0.04 is the fraction of double-positive results that are true cases.

options.text: It is 64%, because disease contributes 0.10 times 0.80 squared and nondisease contributes 0.90 times 0.20 squared to double positives.
options.rationale: The normalized disease mass is 0.064 divided by 0.064 plus 0.036, which equals 0.64.

questions.stem: A robot has an accurate predictor of immediate reward for state-action pairs seen in its log, but a proposed action can move it into states absent from that log. What prevents the reward predictor alone from establishing the action's long-run value?

options.text: The reward predictor converts the task into ordinary supervised learning, so its low logged error identifies the value of each proposed action sequence.
options.rationale: One-step reward labels do not by themselves specify how actions change later states or which later rewards follow.

options.text: Future states come from an external sampling process, so the proposed action affects immediate reward without affecting the later inputs presented to the robot.
options.rationale: The scenario explicitly allows the action to enter new states, making the future state distribution policy-dependent.

options.text: Accurate logged reward predictions identify the proposed policy's value despite missing transitions, since predictive accuracy removes the need for action support.
options.rationale: Logged one-step accuracy does not identify unobserved transition consequences or rewards in unsupported states.

options.text: Long-run value also depends on transition consequences, future policy choices, and adequate support or valid modeling for the states those choices reach.
options.rationale: A return couples immediate reward with the state trajectory generated by actions and the continuation policy.
